source_title: Target Corporation - Form 10-K (Fiscal Year Ended February 2, 2019)
publisher_issuer: Target Corporation (filed with U.S. SEC, EDGAR CIK 0000027419, accession 0000027419-19-000006)
company_context: In February 2017 Target announced it would invest more than $7 billion in capital over three years (and forgo roughly $1 billion in annual operating profit beginning in 2017) to remodel stores, build small-format stores, develop owned brands, and expand same-day digital fulfillment, after a period of soft traffic and competitive pressure from Amazon and Walmart. Fiscal 2018 (year ended February 2, 2019) was the year the strategy delivered its strongest results.
time_period: FY2018 (year ended February 2, 2019), within the FY2017-FY2019 investment program
macro_context: Intense e-commerce competition (Amazon) and discount/grocery pressure (Walmart); industry shift to omnichannel and same-day fulfillment; rising need for digital and store-experience investment to defend traffic.
evidence_summary: Target's heavy reinvestment in stores and digital fulfillment reversed soft demand and restored traffic-driven comparable sales growth. In fiscal 2018, comparable sales increased 5.0%, driven entirely by a 5.0% increase in traffic (transactions), the strongest traffic growth in over a decade. Comparable digital channel sales increased 36%, contributing 1.8 percentage points to comparable sales, marking the fifth straight year of digital comp growth above 25%. Reported net income from continuing operations was $2.94 billion, or $5.51 per diluted share, up from $5.29 per diluted share in fiscal 2017.

source_backed_metrics.investment_program_capital_usd: more than 7 billion over three years (announced Feb 2017)

owner_decision_context: CEO Brian Cornell and the board chose to absorb a large, near-term hit to operating profit (about $1 billion annually) and commit over $7 billion of capital to defend and grow traffic through remodels, small-format stores, owned brands, and same-day services, rather than cut costs and harvest a declining base.
action_taken: Executed the multi-year reinvestment: store remodels, small-format urban/campus stores, expanded same-day fulfillment (Order Pickup, Drive Up, Shipt), and new owned brands.
outcome_evidence: FY2018 delivered 5.0% comp sales on 5.0% traffic growth and 36% digital comp growth, with EPS rising to $5.51 from $5.29, confirming the investment program restored demand and traffic.
source_limitations: WebFetch of sec.gov typically returns HTTP 403 here; figures confirmed verbatim in WebSearch snippets attributed to Target's FY2018 10-K (year ended February 2, 2019) and FY2018 annual report. Note: Target labels this period 'fiscal 2018'; the corresponding 10-K is the one for the year ended February 2, 2019. The $7B investment figure is the announced program size from February 2017, not a single-year cash outlay.
directly_stated: FY2018 comparable sales increased 5.0%, driven by a 5.0% increase in traffic
Comparable digital channel sales increased 36%, contributing 1.8 percentage points to comparable sales
FY2018 was the fifth straight year of comparable digital sales growth above 25%
FY2018 net income from continuing operations was $2.94 billion, or $5.51 per diluted share, versus $5.29 in FY2017
Target announced in February 2017 a plan to invest more than $7 billion over three years
inferred: Comp growth driven entirely by traffic (not just ticket) indicates the investment genuinely re-attracted shoppers, addressing the underlying demand-generation weakness
The combination of restored traffic and rising EPS marks a successful turnaround of the demand and earnings trajectory
why_useful_for_opsiq: Demonstrates a deliberate margin-sacrificing reinvestment that successfully reverses a demand-generation problem, with the proof point being traffic-led (not price-led) comp growth. Tests whether the engine can recognize near-term profit sacrifice as the correct action when it restores durable demand.
